clue.text: He lets no thin diva type forget last aria, perhaps in "Patience"

annotation.answer: THE OPERA AIN'T OVER TIL THE FAT LADY SINGS

definitions.text: He lets no thin diva type forget last aria, perhaps in "Patience"

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the preceding words are only one possible arrangement, so their letters may be set out differently

blocks.clueFragment: He lets no thin diva type forget last aria
blocks.note: all thirty-four letters of the opening words form the fodder

explanation.surface: A producer refuses to let a slim soprano skip the closing number of Gilbert and Sullivan's Patience.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter Bunthorne is named after a character in Patience, which has a stout contralto, Lady Jane. The whole clue both supplies the letters and describes the saying in action.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying means nothing is finished until the very end, pictured as a large soprano's closing number at the opera.

clue.text: Start of the Rangers' collapse; Saints encroach

indicators.note: 'Start of' asks for only the opening letter of the following word
a collapse leaves things fallen in disorder, so the letters before it are jumbled

blocks.note: first letter of 'the'
taken as written
S is the abbreviation for saint, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A football report: Rangers fall apart while Southampton, the Saints, push into their territory.
explanation.definitionFit: To transgress is to overstep a boundary, which is a synonym for intruding or encroaching.

clue.text: O, Anna Neagle! You hadn't a dreadful shape like this

indicators.note: telling her she had no 'a' means one letter A is taken away from her words
something dreadful is in a terrible state, so the remaining letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
the single letter to be removed

explanation.surface: An admirer gushes to the film star Anna Neagle that she never had an ugly figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Anna Neagle was a British film actress of the 1930s-50s. Drop one A from O ANNA NEAGLE and rearrange the ten letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: Enneagonal describes a nine-sided polygon, so it names a kind of geometric shape or figure.

clue.text: Remind me, wasn't he once the Italian PM?

definitions.text: wasn't he once the Italian PM?

blocks.note: to prod someone is to jog their memory
the speaker refers to himself as I

explanation.surface: Someone struggling to recall a name asks whether this man used to lead Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remind me' reads as a plea for help but splits into two pieces of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Romano Prodi served twice as Prime Minister of Italy and also led the European Commission.

clue.text: Kicking oneself in the gaudery, perhaps

indicators.note: 'perhaps' hints that the phrase before it is just one possible ordering of its letters

blocks.note: the three words supply all twelve letters

explanation.surface: Someone berates themselves amid showy finery.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaudery is gaudy display or finery.
explanation.definitionFit: Kicking oneself and rueing the day both describe bitterly regretting something one did.

clue.text: Let oneself down, on the face of it

definitions.text: Let oneself down, on the face of it

blocks.note: surface reading: to disappoint oneself, fall short of one's own standards
setter's reading: lower oneself on a rope literally down a cliff face

explanation.walkthrough: 'On the face of it' sounds like the idiom 'apparently', but here it is a rock face.
explanation.definitionFit: Climbers descend a vertical cliff by rope, lowering themselves down the face.

clue.text: One's sting is in the hell-broth's mild brown brew

definitions.text: One's sting is in the hell-broth

indicators.note: brewing stirs ingredients together, so the preceding letters are mixed up

blocks.note: the two words supply all nine letters

explanation.surface: A witch's cauldron of bland brown liquid with a sting in it.
explanation.walkthrough: In Macbeth the witches' hell-broth includes 'blind-worm's sting'.
explanation.definitionFit: The slow-worm, a legless lizard, is named in the Macbeth witches' recipe for its supposed sting.

clue.text: Albert Einstein's part in designing figure for the Folies-Bergere

indicators.note: 'part in' says only a portion of the following words is wanted, found inside them

blocks.note: spans the end of the first name and the start of the surname

explanation.surface: Einstein, improbably, takes a role in creating a show at the Paris music hall.
explanation.definitionFit: Erté was a Russian-born Art Deco artist who created costumes and sets for the Folies-Bergère revues.

clue.text: Careen this emblem

indicators.note: to careen a vessel is to turn it right over on its side, signalling an overturn

blocks.note: to careen a ship is to keel it over, so the word wanted is keel

explanation.surface: An instruction to tip over some badge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Careen' does double duty: it supplies the word KEEL and, by meaning 'keel over', says that word is turned over to give LEEK.
explanation.definitionFit: The leek is the national emblem of Wales, worn on St David's Day.

clue.text: See 1
See 1
See 1 across
Outback worker needed: 's Mon Oncle available?

blocks.note: the possessive ending taken as a letter
Jacques Tati directed and starred in the film Mon Oncle
something available is on hand

explanation.surface: A job advert in the bush asking whether a French film is in stock.
explanation.walkthrough: The film title stands for its maker, a common crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A station hand is a labourer on an Australian sheep or cattle station, out in the Outback.

clue.text: O, he's the fellow, they say, to chance upon some toothsome relic

indicators.note: 'they say' points to how a word is spoken rather than how it is written

blocks.note: taken as written
a don is a university fellow
taken as written
to light upon something is to chance upon it

explanation.surface: A cry of delight about the man who stumbles on a fossil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toothsome' here means tooth-like, not tasty.
explanation.definitionFit: Odontolite is fossil bone or tooth coloured blue by iron phosphate, also called bone turquoise, a relic of teeth.

clue.text: Saps environmentally friendly fog warnings

blocks.note: green means eco-friendly
foghorns sound warnings at sea

explanation.surface: Eco-friendly foghorns that drain energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saps' looks like a verb meaning drains, but it is the noun for fools.
explanation.definitionFit: A sap is a gullible person, and greenhorns are naive, inexperienced newcomers easily fooled.

clue.text: Take home British, but not English, figure

indicators.note: 'but not' tells us to remove the item named after it

blocks.note: R stands for recipe, Latin for take, on prescriptions
taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: Bringing home a British, not English, figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the E from HOME, then add B.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhomb, or rhombus, is a geometrical figure with four equal sides.

clue.text: Where Beau Nash was immersed in his country residence?

blocks.note: first meaning: a building with public baths, where one is immersed
second meaning: a house in the spa town that was Nash's domain

explanation.walkthrough: Beau Nash was the dandy who ran society in the spa town of Bath, Somerset.
explanation.definitionFit: A building of public baths is where people are immersed, and split in two it is a house in Bath.

clue.text: A lot to ask of a Lilliputian

blocks.note: first meaning: the idiom for an unreasonably demanding request
second meaning, read literally: a command to a six-inch person to be lofty

explanation.walkthrough: Lilliputians are the tiny people of Gulliver's Travels, so the idiom is read word by word as an instruction to grow high.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means a difficult demand, and literally an instruction to gain height suits a tiny person.

clue.text: Pungent plant returned by river with railed transport

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the pieces are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: the Dee is a river in Britain
W is the abbreviation for with
trams run on rails

explanation.surface: A sharp-smelling plant sent back by riverside tram.
explanation.definitionFit: Smartweed is water pepper, a plant of the knotweed family named for its acrid, burning sap.

clue.text: Be affected by food from a runcible spoon

blocks.note: first meaning: walk or speak in a dainty, prissy way
second meaning: in Lear's 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat' they dined on this with a runcible spoon

explanation.walkthrough: 'Be affected by' reads as one phrase, but 'by' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To walk with affected daintiness is one sense; minced meat with quince is what Lear's pair ate.

clue.text: Catches the City unwilling to provide no life cover

blocks.note: to catch a remark is to hear it
EC is the postcode of the City of London
loth is a spelling of loath, reluctant

explanation.surface: The financial City refuses to sell life insurance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Life cover' suggests insurance; 'no life' means a dead body, which this cloth covers.
explanation.definitionFit: A hearse-cloth is a pall draped over a coffin, a covering for someone no longer alive.

clue.text: Firm about revolutionary principles

indicators.note: 'about' places one item around another, enclosing it

blocks.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company
a red is a revolutionary, a communist

explanation.surface: A company wavers over radical ideals.
explanation.definitionFit: A credo is a set of beliefs or guiding tenets, a synonym for one's principles.

clue.text: Fourth World figure in Matabeleland

indicators.note: 'in' says the letters wanted sit inside the following word

blocks.note: lies in the middle of the place name

explanation.surface: A figure from the developing Fourth World in Matabeleland, a region of Zimbabwe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fourth World' looks like economics, but it means the fourth person in the world after Adam, Eve and Cain.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, Abel was born after Adam, Eve and Cain, making him the world's fourth human.

clue.text: Pack member putting one right in the club

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
a bat is a club for hitting a ball

explanation.surface: A Cub Scout is sorted out at the club.
explanation.walkthrough: The Brat Pack was a group of young 1980s Hollywood actors.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the Brat Pack were called brats, so this is one member of that celebrated pack.

clue.text: He admitted all to his circus except miners

definitions.text: He admitted all to his circus

blocks.note: bar means except, as in 'all bar one'
NUM is the National Union of Mineworkers

explanation.surface: A showman lets everyone into his big top apart from coal miners.
explanation.walkthrough: The NUM is the British coal miners' trade union.
explanation.definitionFit: P. T. Barnum was the American showman whose circus welcomed all comers as 'The Greatest Show on Earth'.

clue.text: Conclude with one or less

blocks.note: to infer is to conclude
I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Finish with one item or fewer.
explanation.definitionFit: Inferior means lower in rank or quality, and so lesser.

clue.text: Agitation raised in the 16

blocks.note: first meaning: a nervous fluster
second meaning: soap foam worked up in the place at 16 down, where people bathe

explanation.walkthrough: 16 is the entry at 16 down; the foam is 'raised' by working soap.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a lather means flustered, and lather is also soap froth whipped up when washing.

clue.text: When Guardian readers include Dome developers: what the devil!

indicators.note: 'include' means one group takes something into its midst
developers rework something into a new form, so the letters before it are rearranged

blocks.note: as means when, as in 'as I left'
taken as written
the readers of the Guardian, where the puzzle appears, are us

explanation.surface: Newspaper readers find property developers among them and exclaim in surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: Guardian solvers are 'us' because the puzzle appeared in the Guardian; the exclamation doubles as a definition naming a demon.
explanation.definitionFit: Asmodeus is a demon of Jewish legend, so the answer names a devil.
